en: The Fifty-sixth Fascicle of the *Shi Dunlun Jizhuan Lunben* (The Collected Explanations of Shi Dunlun).

Herein begins the second section, which analyzes the categories and states of the aggregates (*skandha*) with respect to the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Within this, first is the question.
The answer provides a general outline,
referring back to the "Original Section" (Mūlabhāga).
Following this, there are twenty individual question-and-answer sections providing detailed explanations.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanation) states:
"That which is established based on the state of the manifestation of the dominant cause" means that the "cause" is the maturation of the seeds.

Based on defiled dharmas, the seeds of the portion of acquired wholesome roots, of the dharmas of deportment and craftsmanship, and of unwholesome cultivation are established as the causal conditions for the maturation of seeds.

Mastery refers to the seeds of a portion of the wholesome states resulting from application (*prayoga*), as well as those of the wholesome states of deportment (*īryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), for those who have practiced them, and those of transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
It is only through the cultivation of these by means of the causes and efforts of application that they can arise as manifest activity with mastery.
Therefore, mastery and maturation are established.
Among these, only the impure seeds that are currently manifesting—
namely, the two aforementioned types of maturation— do not give rise to manifest activity.
Regarding the meaning, it pertains to practitioners who establish the accomplishment of actualization therein.
As for the statement that among the three mindless states, the attainment of non-conception occurs first here [in the desire realm] and subsequently in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and so forth:
Jingyun: Those who first arise in the desire realm do not necessarily experience retribution;
it is only when they subsequently arise in the form realm that they begin to experience retribution.
One is born into the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) only after relinquishing the body of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As stated in [the *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*] 53:
"Those who practice with inferior capacity will necessarily regress within their present life," and so forth.
It is clearly known that when first arising in the desire realm, one may encounter conditions that cause regression, such that the attainment of the fruit is not certain.
Jì (基) says:
"Because one must first arise from the desire realm, one subsequently arises in the form realm."
Because it encompasses one birth in the form realm,
the meditative absorption entered from the desire realm is karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*).
If one does not further enter absorption in the form realm, [the result follows].
However, in other stages, one receives retribution immediately after being born;
whereas in the desire realm, meditative absorption can result in subsequent retribution,
and in the form realm, one enters absorption even later.
It is clearly known that this person had already been one who had regressed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If he had not regressed, why would he again give rise to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in a different stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Therefore, it is known that one undergoes retribution only after giving rise to meditative absorption in the form realm and so forth once more.
Furthermore, it should be understood that for those in the desire realm who do not fall away, this meditative absorption is exclusively of the nature of retribution upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*).

If this is so, then for those in the desire realm who do fall away, the karma of volition associated with the meditative absorption previously attained remains within their bodies; does this karma not likewise receive its retribution?
The answer is:
If one were to receive the retribution,
one should immediately undergo that fruit for one thousand kalpas.
By entering meditative absorption in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*),
this absorption induces a rebirth-retribution (*upapadyavedanīya*) lasting for five hundred kalpas.
Once these are completed, the karma of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) matures and one must again undergo its fruit for another five hundred kalpas.
Should one then receive that fruit for a thousand kalpas?
If the meditative concentration of the form realm induces that birth-retribution while the karma of the desire realm and so forth simultaneously induce their individual retributions, [then...]
This karma of the desire realm thus becomes one that ripens in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*).
At present, this fruit is not experienced because this karma has not yet matured and is weak due to being [still] in the state of the next birth. If that is so, then...
It should then follow that this is a retribution of indefinite timing; it may be regarded as a retribution arising outside of the Mahāyāna.

That which is experienced later is all termed "later" (paścima-vedanīya); even if one has already passed through hundreds of thousands of births before finally experiencing the retribution therein, it is still called a "later retribution."
If that were so, then when one subsequently desires to be born there, one must first attain meditative concentration;
having attained this concentration, its cessation and subsequent birth there would constitute "retribution upon rebirth" (upapadyavedanīya).
Question: At what time is the retribution for prior karma experienced?
Answer: It is called "subsequent retribution" because it is experienced as a distinct retribution within that very same life.

If that is so, then when one is born in the desire realm and enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), is the experience of distinct retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*) also called "karma with subsequent retribution" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*)?
The Tripitaka Master said:
If a person who has regressed subsequently arises in the form realm,
their prior karma of the desire realm is categorized as having a fixed time [of maturation] but an indefinite retribution.
Furthermore, this text states that "arising here first" refers to entering meditative absorption.
"Subsequently regarding form" means that, as read in the subsequent text, one desires to experience the retribution of subsequently produced form;
it does not mean entering meditative absorption in the form realm subsequently.
If [it were] already established that one can manifest [the attainment] in all places, [then this would be redundant].
If, according to the principle of the *anuvartaka* (concomitant) system, the teaching of the ālayavijñāna has not yet been established,

then a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who has previously abandoned the afflictions of the three dhyānas in the desire realm and suppressed the afflictions from the fourth dhyāna upward may enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Having subsequently emerged from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and been reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one again gives rise to the meditative attainment of cessation.
Fearing that [the continuum] would become a total annihilation, one must rely upon the physical body (*rūpakāya*) to enter the attainment;
therefore, the meditative attainment of cessation does not arise within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If one establishes the teaching of the ālayavijñāna based on the principle of ultimate reality,
it is said that although those born in the formless realm lack a physical body and have ceased the six consciousnesses,
they nevertheless give rise to the meditative attainment of cessation by relying upon the ālayavijñāna.
Therefore, it manifests in all places within the three realms.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the teaching of the ālayavijñāna was not established based on the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other such scriptures.
The attainment of cessation arises only by relying on the rūpakāya. However,
according to the teachings established in the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra and other texts that posit the ālayavijñāna,
the attainment of cessation can arise even for those born in the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu).
Regarding the statement, "The state of cessation of names within the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings that have already arisen," Jing says:
"In the Abhidharma,
this refers to the two mindless meditative attainments and the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings."
All say that it is established by the cessation of the non-perpetually active mind and mental factors;
thus, we know that the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñika) is established solely on the basis of the seeds of the resultant consciousness of those gods.
Because the essence of that seed’s continuous succession from beginning to end is a resultant neutral state (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), the Unconscious Heaven (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) is established therein;
therefore, the Unconscious Heaven is also called "maturation" (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, in this heaven, because all are designated by the name "aggregates of clouds" (*megha-skandha*), the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) are established based on the state of cessation.
If one establishes these based on the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), they are designated as being "above" [the realm of desire] by means of the four aggregates.
The text should rather state that the four aggregates manifesting [there] are established as "superior," and it should not say they are established only at the stage of cessation (*nirodha-avasthā*).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"Because within those heavens, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is established as 'non-conceptual' (*asaṃjñika*)."
This is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, it is now stated that the volition (*cetanā*) which conceives of aversion toward thought is able to extinguish non-conception (*asaṃjñi*);
therefore, it is said: "The volition capable of inducing the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) brings about its corresponding maturation (*vipāka*)."
It is stated that the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) can extinguish non-conceptuality (*asaṃjñika*). Cè (Cè) says:
"In principle, it is through the attainment of non-conceptualization that one attains the extinction of non-conceptuality."
The Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra), relying on the basis [of the action], states that volition (*cetanā*) can bring about the fruit of those heavens.
Ji says: "Volition associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can extinguish individual retribution."
Regarding the statement, "Having given rise to subsequent perceptions,
one passes away from there," Jing says: "This passage contradicts what is stated below."
It states that for those non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), the eye and other sense organs are at all times not the basis for contact.

Furthermore, the aforementioned four propositions state that the ālayavijñāna is established [as their support] while the six consciousnesses are not; this refers to the Heaven of Non-perception and so forth.
How can this text state that there is consciousness at the time of death? The explanation is as follows:

because in the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva) there is frequently an absence of mind, the six consciousnesses and the sense organs such as the eye do not constitute the bases for contact and so forth.
The Tripitaka Master further stated:
"Regarding those who, after having been conceived, pass away from that realm,
they are called 'now come' by way of analogy to those who have already descended from the heavens."
Just as it was previously stated regarding the naming [of the intermediate state], so it is here as well.
It should be said that after passing away from that life, at the time of taking rebirth, the mental perception (*manovijñāna*) is precisely arising.
It is said that their "arising" is called "having already arisen," because the Western linguistic convention reverses the order: first one guides [the mind],
and subsequently, at the time of taking birth, once the mental perception has already arisen, one then guides it toward the non-percipient existence (*asaṃjñisattva*) and passes away from there.
However, this does not equal the previous explanation.

For both the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Abhidharma* state that there are nine types of death-minds, all of which give rise to self-love (*ātmasneha*) at the moment of death to ensure the continuity of the present life.
Jñānaprabha says:
In this regard, according to the gateway of reasoning,
in the Mahāyāna, that fruit is without mind both at its initial arising and at the end of life.
How is this known?
As the following passage states: "During one period, there is no mind, and there is only form," this refers to those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Thus, it is known that there is only form and no mind.
Furthermore, there is the case where one has a mind at the moment of initial birth, but subsequently lacks a mind.
In the Western regions (India), it is universally held that when karma produces a result, it produces a result of non-mind rather than a result of mind; therefore, they are without mind.
Furthermore, one should read this passage at length as follows: "That is to say, once [a being] has been born, they immediately pass away from that state;
having already established the designation of 'intermediate existence' (antarābhava), the sentient being within that intermediate existence then passes away from it."
This is the doctrine of the Mahāyāna school and not the tenet of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), Jing says:

When the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not called "maturation-indeterminate" (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) but is instead called "indeterminate by its own nature" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*),
it means that this very maturation is, from the perspective of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), indeterminate by its own nature.

However, it is known that "indeterminate by nature" (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*) is broad and pervasive, encompassing the five sense faculties, the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), and so forth;
whereas "maturation" (*vipāka*) is narrow, being restricted solely to the ālayavijñāna.
Master Ji says:

"In this context, the initial passage states that 'the duration of maturation is determined,' etc., which indicates that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) appears to be exclusively a collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*).

However, the subsequent passage states that among the three types [of life], there are further distinctions based on being determinate or being agreeable/disagreeable; from this, one knows that it also extends to individual retribution (*prātyātmikavipāka*)."
Furthermore, as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"The timing of the abiding of the six bases of maturation is determined," which likewise encompasses both collective and individual retributions.
This is because [the ālayavijñāna] is not established upon the eighth consciousness.
If it were otherwise,
as Master Jùn said:
Just as with the seeds of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
although it is said that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are preeminent by virtue of being beginningless and natural,
the term "mind" (*manas*) here refers exclusively to the sixth base.
This is also like that:
although it is called the "six bases," the intent refers specifically to the sixth base;
thus, it is merely a provisional designation for the total retribution upon the eighth consciousness.
The same applies to the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and so forth.
Regarding "being determinate or indeterminate," this refers to those who die prematurely versus those who do not, and those with a determinate lifespan versus those with an indeterminate lifespan.
Feeling that which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant is the fruit of both the happy and miserable destinies.
This is because it is established according to the number of years, kalpas, and so forth.
This refers to the division of the lifespan limit, such as one kalpa or the like.
Regarding the "homogeneity of the group" (nikāya-sabhāga), Jing says:
Regarding the establishment of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) based on the similar states of sentient beings,
homogeneity is established generally across the three natures and the five categories.
As for "homogeneity of genus" (*nikāya-sabhāgatā*):
The four classes, such as the kṣatriyas and so forth, are similar in their generic types.
As for their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
within each respective class, there is subsequently the commonality of male and female, as well as of firmness and softness.
Among males, those who naturally delight in virtue and habitually practice non-virtue are all termed "homogeneous by nature" (*svabhāva-sabhāgatā*).
Those who share the same livelihood through arts and crafts are termed "homogeneous by occupation" (*śilpa-karmasthāna-ājīva-sabhāgatā*).
It sustains life, performs labor, and produces skillful crafts;
it establishes the commonality of group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*). Baso says:
It is established only as belonging to the category of sentient beings, and not as non-sentient.
Why? Because there is a distinction between those who go toward rebirth and those who do not.
This is established solely upon the category of sentient beings;
among those who have been born,
there are no such sentient beings at present.
Arising at each moment and continuing as a stream of its own kind is called "arising by continuity."
The *kalala* and so forth are called "birth by way of stages.
Question:
Regarding that which arises in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*):
when a phenomenon arises from causes and conditions in a single thought-moment, it is precisely that phenomenon which arises.
Why is it called "provisional" (*prajñapti*)?
The commentary explains:
Within the designation "arising," there is no distinct arising of arising;
rather, one establishes that "arising" as a conventional construct based on the occurrence of the dharmas of form and mind.
Therefore, birth is a designation.
Regarding aging: there is the aged who are of a different nature [from the one born].
Regarding "the aged who undergo transformation with different natures before and after," this refers to the transformation of the ten stages.
Regarding the "aging of enjoyment":
as one enjoys the six sense objects, they gradually decline; this is what is meant by "abiding in the midst."
"Abiding by established conventions" refers to practices such as laws and regulations that continue to be observed in the world without interruption;
this is called abiding by established conventions.
Among impermanent things,
that which perishes does so in a single thought-moment.
Transformation refers to the transition from youth to old age.
Separation refers to...
The loss of wealth and the dispersal of one's kin are called the three kinds within the body.
Jingyun: If one speaks of the conventional dharma that is the collection of a jar and a basin, it is called a "provisional designation of a name-body" (*prajñapti-saṃjñā-kāya*).

If one speaks generally of common characteristics such as blue and so forth in relation to the aforementioned conventional dharma of collection, it is a "real entity name-body" (*dravya-saṃjñā-kāya*).
To speak of the dharmas known in common by the former two [classes of beings] is called the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) of common understanding;
if one speaks of the dharmas not known in common by the former two, it is called the "name-body" of worldly uncommon understanding.
Ce says: To speak of white as black and so forth is called a "provisional designation" (prajñapti-nāman);
to speak of white as white and so forth is called a "substantial designation" (dravya-nāman).
At the beginning of the eon, names such as "Mount Meru" were established collectively and are thus commonly understood by the world;
all other names, however, change according to whim and therefore are not commonly understood.
Regarding the distinction herein, [it extends] up to "that which is comprised by sounds and comprised by syllables.
Jing says: "In the Sanskrit language, this is called the *Chandana-śāstra* (Treatise on Prosody)."
This is translated as "Voice" (*svara*). Regarding the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma, there are three types of voice:
namely, masculine, feminine, and neither-masculine-nor-feminine.
Among these three voices, it must possess both long and short prosodic tones to be complete.
This "foot" (*pada*) is comprised of names and sounds.
In the linguistic system of the Western Regions, a phrase must consist of four syllables to constitute a single foot;
thus, it is comprised of names.
These four types all explain the meaning of the phrases.
Jì (基) says:
There are two kinds of phrases: namely, the general heading and the detailed explanation.
The letter "Tai" has two aspects.
This refers to the fourteen root vowels,
namely *a*, *ā*, and so forth;
and the consonants refer to the thirty-four letters.
*Kakāka* and so forth are also included within the category of sounds;
that is, the *Chandana-śāstra*.
When there are men, women, and so forth, each having seven revolutions, they constitute sound;
that which is subsumed under syllables is what is called "speech-sound and syllable."
Regarding the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*),
Jing says: "In this context,
'attainment' (*prāpti*) is established, but 'non-attainment' (*aprāpti*) is not."
It is simply said that the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) consists in not attaining the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
By citing this non-attainment of the noble dharmas, one illustrates all types of non-attainment;
thus, it also corresponds to the meaning of that non-attainment.
Jizang said:
"In the Hīnayāna, [the afflictions] are exclusively of the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) and are abandoned through the path of cultivation;
in the Mahāyāna, it cannot be thus."
Because there is no distinct nature of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*),
the "nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*) established in the *Purāṇa-saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya* is not subsumed under any [of the categories of] non-acquisition.
Because the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is restricted [to a specific state],
the *Abhidharmakośa* now establishes "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) as a distinct category;
thus, the nature of an ordinary person is included within non-acquisition.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is itself the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*); within non-acquisition, there is a broad scope that encompasses all forms of non-acquisition.
According to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the acquisition of dharmas occurs prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with the dharma itself.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exists only prior to or posterior to a dharma; there is no non-acquisition that is simultaneous with the dharma.
This is because when a dharma is present before one, it is necessarily termed "attained" (*samanvāgata*), and attainment is synonymous with acquisition (*prāpti*).
Thus, acquisition is indeed simultaneous with the dharma.
The non-acquisition of a dharma that is not currently manifest is called "non-acquisition concomitant with the dharma" (*dharmasamanvāgama-aprāpti*).
Even when there is no acquisition of a present [dharma], there must necessarily be a non-acquisition concomitant with that dharma, because it constitutes its possession;
however, if [the dharma] pertains to the past or future, there is indeed non-acquisition.
In the Mahāyāna, there is only acquisition co-existent with the dharma (*dharmasahaja-prāpti*),
because acquisition is established as being dependent upon a basis.
There is no prior or subsequent acquisition or non-acquisition of a non-existent dharma.
Since it is established that non-possession (*aprāpti*) exists only with respect to the past and the future, there is no such thing as a "non-existent conception" (*abhāva-saṃjñā*).
This is because non-possession is not established upon a non-existent entity (*abhāva-dharma*);
if there were a dharma that could be acquired at one time and later lost, then non-possession would be possible.
Because it is established in relation to the past and the future,
the Mahāyāna does not establish "the nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva) as something distinct from non-attainment (aprāpti).
This nature is established precisely upon the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya-kleśa).
Because one has not yet attained the various noble dharmas such as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
if one has not attained the path of seeing, one cannot be established upon any of the noble paths.

Since the attainment of even a single portion [of that path] means the remainder belongs to this same category, the path of seeing is not designated as the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
It pervades the three realms.
When one is free from the defilements of those stages, it is also called "a portion of tranquility.
Furthermore, it can be explained according to its meaning as a phenomenon that exists based on seeds.
It is also of the nature of being obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
One cannot grasp the general meaning of all phenomena while on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the three vehicles.

If one were unable to attain the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) or the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), then the path of seeing itself would have to be designated by this [obscured-indeterminate] nature.
It may also be said that they are abandoned at the time of relinquishing the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) while in the state of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Within the process of transmigration,
they are abandoned as they arise and perish moment by moment, subsequently passing away.
The cycling from moment to moment is called "momentary transmigration.
The coming and going between the three realms is called "successive transmigration through birth."
The dharmas of the three natures arise as a continuous flow;
this is called the mutual transition between defilement and purity. This occurs within the category of "distinctness."
Jingyun: To say that characteristics are fixedly distinct is like [the distinction between] blue and yellow, and so forth.
The certainty of difference in cause is due to the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome;
the certainty of difference in fruit is...
Regarding the distinction between suffering and pleasure, Master Ji says:
"Their characteristics are definitively different."
This refers to the essence, characteristics, and so forth within cause and effect,
as well as within association. Jing says:
Goodness brings about the cessation of suffering,
while evil invites it; when the causes and conditions are complete, [the result follows].
This is called "correspondence through conjunction.
For example, it refers to one who, having attained stability at a later time, abandons delusions and returns to rely upon the former skillful means of reciting the sutras;
thus, one must eventually attain [realization] through this process.
This is called "correspondence with skillful means.
Whatever good or evil one performs,
it accords with the established laws.
That which brings about accomplishment is called "correspondence with what is to be done" (*kārya-saṃprayoga*). Ji says:

"Concordance with skillful means" refers to the fact that preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) and all fundamental matters are termed "skillful means," as they accord with the principle of appropriateness.
This refers to wisdom that accords with principle.
Regarding the swiftness of momentum among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), it is as follows:
In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, six hundred cycles of arising and ceasing pass.
As for the speed of human effort (*puruṣakāra-vega*),
it is like the swiftness of the three karmas of a person who has severed their roots [of virtue] within the world.
Regarding the swiftness of the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*):
it is like reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven in the mere time it takes to bend or extend one’s arm,
and so forth, within the sequence.
Regarding the sequence of momentary flux:
it is the sequence of the flux of preceding moments.
Regarding the sequence of the internal body's flux: [it is as follows].
Just as within a single body there is a sequence of ten stages,
so too is the sequence of the flow of conditioned activity established;
it is like the external vessel-world being established through its successive arrangement.
Regarding the timing,
there are three explanations from the West.
First, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that "the seed and the fruit coexist."
This is based on the fact that both [the cause and the effect] must exist simultaneously;
although the causal conditions are absent at the time of the vajra-mind, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) still exists.
Therefore, the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) has not yet arisen at that time.
Regarding the five types in the second clause:
they consist of those within the womb during the first four stages before the eye-faculty has arisen,
as well as ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
It is always the second phrase.
Even during the fifth stage and after emerging from the womb, although one has obtained the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya), [it is not yet fully functional].
Because it has been damaged by him,
it is said that "either it is lost after having arisen,
or one has never possessed the eye-faculty from the very beginning."
Alternatively, that which has arisen and ceased, having entered the past, lacks the substance of the eye and is termed "immediately ceased.
As for "both being absent," this refers to an arhat who has lost his eyesight.
Either the eye has never arisen from the beginning,
or that Arhat is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
or they enter the remainderless nirvāṇa (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) from a body belonging to the three realms.

Regarding the body element (*kāyadhātu*), there is nothing that comes from elsewhere nor is it produced anew; as for the remaining [elements] associated with the body, they are likewise as appropriate.
Furthermore, the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) exists in the two lower realms, and there too it does not exist at a time when it has not yet arisen.
Nor is there any case where [the mind] has arisen and then perished;
rather, it simply passes away immediately after arising and enters the past. If one were to formulate this in terms of the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi):
It should be said that the body is not the element of the body (*kāyadhātu*).

This refers to the final body of an Arhat, as well as the final relinquishing of the body by those in training (*śaikṣa*) who, passing away from the two lower realms, are reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There is the body-element that is not the body,
namely: the body-faculty of the two lower realms that has just ceased and entered the past,
as well as those born in the formless realm.
The remaining two phrases may be understood.
Regarding the detailed explanation of the four external elements as appropriate:
if the four objects of the lower realm are constantly present.
If one is in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is no odor or fragrance;
however, visible form (rūpa) and tangibility (spraṣṭavya) are always present. This can be understood through the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
This refers to the final matter of an Arhat,
as well as the final matter relinquished by a trainee (*śaikṣa*) at the moment of passing away from the two lower realms to be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

There are those who possess the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) but are not of the nature of form (*arūpin*); this refers to the relative presence of the four sense-faculties during the first four stages of gestation within the womb, as well as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The remaining two phrases may be understood accordingly.
The same applies to the three cases of odor, taste, and touch.

Regarding the treatise that states, "Or else this eye necessarily ceases immediately thereafter," the Tripiṭaka Master further examined the Sanskrit manuscript and found that the word "necessarily" (必) was not present; thus, it accords better with reason.
Why is this? If there were the word "exists," it would mean that the eye has not yet ceased in the present.
It cannot be that they are entirely non-existent simply because they are not eyes.
If there were no such thing as the "eye-seed," it would not constitute an element (*dhātu*).
Is it not the case that even if seeds exist, they cannot be called an element if they are incapable of producing an eye?
The Tripitaka Master relates two Western traditions.
According to one tradition:
if one is certainly not to be reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), [one does not need to cultivate the fourth dhyāna].
Since the seed of the eye has already been abandoned,
it is not called the "eye-element.
Question:
If that is so, then those who turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle will never again give rise to the untainted [attainments] of the two vehicles.
At that time, when they have not yet arisen, there is no untainted (anāsrava) state.
However, since the previous seeds have already been abandoned, should this [new] arising be considered different from them?
Regarding this, the Tripiṭaka Master offers two interpretations.
This has one meaning:
at the time of entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), when it is essential, the preceding thought first abandons the inferior untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*),
and immediately thereafter, the untainted [seeds] of a bodhisattva arise in succession.
First interpretation:
Prior to the stages (bhūmi), one immediately gives rise to the bodhisattva’s untainted cultivation of Mahāyāna practices;
at the moment the untainted seeds of the two vehicles give rise to the great resolve (mahācitta), they are abandoned and do not come to fruition.
The second explanation states:
it merely abandons the functional capacity for the manifestation of birth.
Master Ce asked:
If it is admitted that there is no seed for those non-returners in the formless realm,
why is it that the eye-seed already produced and the eye-seed not yet produced do not both exist? Answer:
Because no further fruit arises,
one who has just been born into the formless realm immediately abandons the seed.
Question:
If that is so, could it not also be said that the seeds of affliction possessed by Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward are not established, because they serve no purpose?
The explanation says:
The seeds have two functions:
first, the function of producing fruits;
second, the function of obstructing the path.
Although the seeds of the afflictions in that state lack their former function,
they still possess their subsequent function;
therefore, they are not abandoned.
Master Ji says that, as in the second fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are two interpretations of the term "dispute" (*vivāda*),
because both seeds and manifest activities are termed "elements" (*dhātu*). For this reason,
he provides a harmonizing explanation of this passage.
The Master Jayasena takes this as proof that the arising of the seeds and the manifestation [of the dharmas] do not occur simultaneously.
However, there is no fault here, as the eye in its state of manifestation is superior and thus constitutes the "element" (dhātu).
Furthermore, one should also formulate four minor tetralemmas regarding external objects, such as "attaining the eye but not the visible form," and so forth.
That is to say, when the eye does not transform into form, one attains the eye but does not attain form;
for one who lacks the eye, there is only the eighth characteristic of form, and thus one attains form but does not attain the eye.
Both are accomplished; both are not accomplished, and so forth.
The fourth [section] clarifies the homogeneous (sabhāga) and the partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
When the sense organs and consciousnesses alike apprehend their objects,
the organs are termed "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Because consciousness is common to the sense faculties,
those mental factors within the dharma-element that are like the mind are "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Other phenomena such as form and so forth are not common [to the faculties], and thus, like the five objects of sense, they are "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
Furthermore, another interpretation is that the Hīnayāna school establishes the existence of the three time periods and asserts that the seven mental elements (cittadhātu) do not arise in the future.
That which is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga) refers to the seven mental elements (manodhātu) of the present;
these are termed "homogeneous."
In the Mahāyāna, past and future phenomena do not exist.
If one distinguishes the meanings of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) separately, only those in the present exist.
Consciousness arises in the present.
It must necessarily have a "month" [as its basis];
thus, there is no distinction between the homogeneous (sabhāga) and the partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga) regarding the six objects, such as visible form and the rest.
However, they lack the activity of apprehending external objects,
nor do they distinguish between the state of being "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga);
they simply manifest as the five sense-faculties without depending on other conditions.
Within the continuity of its own kind,

that which possesses consciousness but has not yet relied upon it for the function of apprehending objects is termed "homogeneous" (sabhāga); that which lacks consciousness and has not yet relied upon it for the function of non-apprehension of objects is [termed] "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
This is called "homogeneity" (sabhāga).
The Abhidharma-piṭaka, Chapter Four, states:
"Because the sense faculties function in a manner similar to their corresponding consciousnesses, they are designated as 'homogeneous' (sabhāga) based on this meaning of similarity."
Because the sense faculties do not combine with consciousness,
they arise solely within their own continuum; thus,
the characteristics of the faculties are similar.
This is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
This explains that the five sense faculties arise as a single continuum;
when they are conjoined with consciousness, they function as consciousness.
That which is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga) does not conjoin with consciousness; that which does not so conjoin is called "non-homogeneous" (tat-sabhāga).
Regarding the five objects, such as form, in relation to the five consciousnesses, there is neither conjunction nor non-conjunction.
If they are considered to be of the same category (sabhāga),
they lack any substantial entity at the time when those six consciousnesses have not yet arisen.
It is impossible to distinguish whether they belong to the same or different categories;
if they have already arisen,
they possess only functional utility.
Nor can they constitute two categories.
How, then, could one distinguish between those that are homogeneous and those that are non-homogeneous?
Therefore, only the five sense-faculties can constitute these two categories.
One must not explain the future as being non-existent, as the Hinayana does; rather, it must be understood according to the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā*.

Just as when one perceives the past or the future, there arises a corresponding mind that manifests in the likeness of the past or future, so too within this very consciousness there exist the functional capacities (*śakti*) for the past and the future.
Now, precisely because the present moment resembles that [past or future state], the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) allows for the designation of "past" and "future";
however, these two dharmic characteristics apply only to the present.
That is to say, present phenomena that are about to cease are called "past";
those not yet ceased are called "future";
and those currently arising are called "present."
The three time periods are established based on the characteristics of phenomena within the present dharma.
The three supernormal powers (abhijñā) are explained as three;
these are the powers of the various Buddhas and others.
It is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) that they appear as having counterparts.
That is to say, a present phenomenon is called "past" because it has already possessed functional capacity,
and it is called "future" because it will possess functional capacity.
Even within the present life itself, there is such functional capacity that it is figuratively described as the three times,
as previously explained in the section on "Directions."
The Abhidharma also states:
"The various directions are established solely based on the causes and effects of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
If one refers to that which exists within a direction as a 'direction,' [then it is so designated]."
The four aggregates are also called "directions.
Therefore, the preceding text states:
"In whatever place or in whatever birth one may reside."

This is precisely what is subsumed within this context. Regarding the statement that "numbers are established based on the stages of formal expression according to the Dharma": * **依 (yi):** To rely upon; to depend on. * **法 (fa):** The Dharma; the teaching; the principle; the method. * **齊量 (qíliàng):** Equal measure; standardization; uniformity. * **表 (biǎo):** To express; to manifest; to represent. * **了 (liǎo):** To understand; to comprehend; to clarify. * **分位 (fēnwèi):** Stages; positions; states; divisions. * **立 (lì):** To establish; to set up; to institute. * **數 (shù):** Number; enumeration. **Translation:** Regarding the phrase "establishing numbers based on the stages of formal expression according to the Dharma": it means that one relies upon the Dharma—the principles of the teaching—to establish numerical categories based on the standardized measures and the stages of clear expression. This refers to the process by which numerical designations are applied to phenomena through a systematic and uniform method of representation.
Alternatively, they are provisionally established as numbers based on the state of mental intention or vocal action that makes [the meaning] manifest.
Regarding "in the midst of harmony," Jingyun says: "The assembly."
Just as a great gathering of people is conventionally designated by the name "assembly," so too is that which is a unification of a single meaning.
Just as the members of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) must be complete,
so too may all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise together toward a single object.
"Object" (*viṣaya*) is here termed "referent" (*artha*).
The harmony of name and meaning.
As for the harmony of perfection,
it is like the perfection of a worldly retinue.
Master Ji says:
"The first is 'harmony of purpose,' which means relying upon the same performed task."
Perfection and harmony refer to the time when ultimate attainment is reached;
within that which was previously disharmonious.
Regarding "states" (avasthā) and "distinctions" (viśeṣa), Jing says:
"If the preceding and succeeding states do not harmonize."
Whether identical or differentiated, they stand side by side without merging.
Ce (Cemei) says:
"If it refers to states (avasthā):"
Regarding the three preceding stages:
if there is a distinction,
then there is a distinction among these three stages.
This is the third section from here on:
the analysis of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) by way of various categories.
Within this, there is first a detailed explanation.
The subsequent summary,
in its commentary,
first analyzes the aggregates through nineteen questions, such as "having form" and "being visible."
In the latter [section], there are questions concerning "having form" and so forth, which serve to clarify the meaning of "being formless" and so forth.
Among these, the first three types are subtle.
As explained in the fifty-fourth fascicle,

the meaning of "coarse" (*audārika*) here refers to that which is coarse within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), specifically the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*); it is not that which is subtle (*sūkṣma*).
It is not that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) alone is coarse and large.
Regarding the explanation of "contaminated" (*sāsrava*), it says:
"accompanied by heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya-anuṣakta*) and so forth.
It is accompanied by the heavy residues of the various afflictions;
it is not an antidote,
but arises from the afflictions.
This is the meaning of being with outflows (sāsrava). There are four faults:
first, lack of tranquility (aśānti).
The text below states that these are produced by the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
This refers precisely to the nature of the manifest afflictions (*kleśa*) as explained in the treatise.
The Tripitaka Master said:
Because the afflictions manifest, they disturb the faculties and so forth, which is termed "non-quiescence.
Second, there are internal and external transformations;
as it says below, "the various affairs of the afflictions follow upon what has been done by the afflictions."
This refers to the objective bases upon which the various afflictions depend.

Because such greed, hatred, and so forth arise, there now occurs the transformation of both the internal and external; that is, the transformation of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
These sense faculties and objects are termed "bases" (*vastu*).
Third, the arousal of unwholesome conduct.
As stated below, it is produced by the causes and conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is because the afflictions serve as the causes and conditions.
It gives rise to misconduct;
misconduct is produced by the afflictions;
these are the four causes of appropriation.
The text below states that it "induces future existence," as can be understood from the passage itself.
It also mentions "craving for the flavor of contention" (*saraṇa-rasa-tṛṣṇā*) and so forth.
This is explained in detail in works such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
The Tripiṭaka Master states:
"That which is 'contentious' refers exclusively to the essence of hatred (*dveṣa*), yet it pervades all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena."
Relishing arises solely by taking the internal body as its object;
indulgence arises solely by taking external sensual desires as its object;
this text alone exists within the desire realm.
Jingyun: "Attachment to flavor (āsvādanasamprayukta) pervades all three realms;
indulgence (gardha) exists only in the desire realm."
Regarding the statement that "the basis of conceptual proliferation is the world":
that which can give rise to the false grasping of discrimination is called the basis of conceptual proliferation.
Regarding the explanation of the three periods of time:

why is it that causes and effects already experienced are called the past, those not yet experienced are called the future, and causes already experienced together with results not yet experienced are called the present?
The terms "future" and "past" are both explained in reference to simultaneous cause and effect, as well as to cases where the fruit has already been utilized;
the term "present," however, refers to cases of outflowing cause and effect that occur at different times.
This refers to past effects and present [causes], which are not simultaneous causes and effects;
there are no effects in the present.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is based on a specific sense.
Therefore, this differs in meaning from what is explained in the third fascicle of the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Among the internal and external inquiries,
the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are all included within that [category] as internal appropriation (*ādhyātmikam upādānam*).
The six internal sense bases (ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana) are all comprised of the five material sense organs (rūpīndriya), their corresponding four objects (viṣaya), and internal sound;

furthermore, they comprise the mental sense base (manas-indriya), the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (vedanā-, saṃjñā-, and saṃskāra-skandha), as well as matter produced by meditative mastery (dhyāna-vaśitā-rūpa).
Therefore, it is said:
"One part of one aggregate is external.
This refers to taking only the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), which are insentient, from within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Therefore, it is said that one part [is coarse].
The aggregates of the three evil destinies are called coarse;
those of humans and devas are subtle.
Although the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) are impermanent,
they are neither suffering nor impure;
they are sublime.
Regarding the meaning of "distance" as the separation of location, movement, time, and direction:
Jing says that this refers to distance of location.
As with India and China, those places are distant from one another due to being separated by mountains and rivers;
as for the time of going and coming:
The past is distant because it is remote from the present;
the future is distant because it has not yet reached the present.
Cè (Cè) says:
Regarding the explanation of the location:
previously, it was explained that the distance between going and coming involves a temporal interval;
now, it is stated that there is a temporal interval.
This explains and establishes the past and future,
as well as spatial separation;
it explains and establishes location.
The Minor Treatise explains the four kinds of distance:
namely, those of place, time, nature, and characteristic.
For example, there is no distance between good and evil, nor between form and color.
Although they arise within the same body,
because their natures are different,
they are said to be "distant by nature."
For example, although the four great elements exist within a single body,
they are called "distant" by way of their characteristics because their qualities— solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion— are distinct.
In this context, the two [types of beings] are briefly not distinguished.
Among those bound to the three realms,
regarding the statement "born in the desire realm and not yet having obtained the antidote":

In the first stage, one has not yet attained the untainted [dharmas] (*anāsrava*) nor the antidote to the mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-citta*), and thus possesses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the desire realm.
Alternatively, in the second stage, when these have been attained, one possesses only the matter (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) of the desire realm.
"Those who have already emerged" refers to those who,
during the third period, emerge from the outflow-free (anāsrava) and form-sphere (rūpadhātu) meditative absorptions while still possessing the five aggregates of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
In the passage concerning the manifestation during the three times,
the forms of the external receptacle world and the form realm are already fully included.
Regarding the statement that one who has already attained the antidote to the form realm enters that meditative absorption:
when one’s body is in the desire realm yet attains the formless absorptions and enters those meditative states,
this is the first period, during which only the contaminated seeds of the form realm are established.
Alternatively, for one who has been born there but has not yet attained the antidote,
being in the form realm while not yet having attained a mind of the formless realm—
this is the second period, during which the five aggregates of form are fully present.
Or, having already emerged,
one whose body is in the form realm attains a mind of the formless realm;
having already emerged, one practices dharmas associated with the form realm.
This is the third period.
Regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
if one who has already attained the antidote enters that meditative absorption while their body remains in a lower stage, and they enter an untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*), this is the first period.
It merely becomes a seed bound to the formless realm;
or, it is the second period when one is born there and has not yet attained the antidote.
Those born in the formless realm who have not yet attained the ultimate antidote possess the four aggregates of the formless realm;
or those who have already emerged from it— namely,
Arhats of the formless realm who have attained the ultimate antidote of the formless realm.
Having already explained the emergence of factors bound to the formless realm,
this is the third period.
Furthermore, there is a distinction regarding that which is associated with pliancy (praśrabdhi) and samādhi.
Regarding the samādhi of "dispersing simplicity" (*jian-san sanmo-di*) and its retinue as well as its fruit, Jing says:
Furthermore, the five aggregates that are wholesome are called the "retinue.
The maturation produced by both the meditative absorption and its retinue is called the "resultant dharma. Kī says:
The "retinue" refers to the co-arising mind and mental factors.
Those "dharmas that are its fruit" are specifically the restraint associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*) and the matter that is the fruit of the meditative object.
These are established as being bound to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth.
The remainder are bound to the desire realm.
As for those belonging to the afflictions of the form realm:
all contaminated phenomena of the form realm arise from the afflictions of the form realm.
Furthermore, because the characteristics of the causes and effects of the afflictions that arise again are distinct,
it is said that these afflictions pertaining to form are contrary to those of the desire realm.

This refers to that which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the meaning of being "subsumed by that" which is free from the afflictions of form: it means being free from the afflictions of form.
This refers to the formless defilements and all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) arising from those formless defilements;
the fruit belongs to its cause.
This is bound by the formless realm;
therefore, it is said that the meaning of "comprised therein" refers to being bound by the formless realm.
Among the three natures:
That which can induce a pleasant retribution in the future is tainted wholesome karma; furthermore,
that which serves as the antidote to afflictions and suffering [is untainted].
This is untainted wholesome [action] that can induce a painful retribution;
this is unwholesome karma.
The arousal of misconduct is unwholesome affliction;
it is free from fault.
This refers to untainted virtue (*anāsrava-kuśala*).
Regarding that which is the antidote to faults and conforms to qualities:
this means that being the antidote to faults and conforming to qualities constitutes tainted virtue (*sāsrava-kuśala*).
Regarding the three types of learners (*śaikṣa*): as stated in the Abhidharma,
"Whatever wholesome dharmas belong to one seeking liberation constitute the meaning of being a learner."
From the stage of accumulating the provisions onward, one is called a "seeker of liberation.
Ten elements (dhātus), four bases (āyatanas), and a portion of the aggregates (skandhas) belong to those in training (śaikṣa).
All wholesome phenomena belonging to one who has attained the ultimate perfection of all points of training (śikṣāpada) are those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
That is to say, a portion of the ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and all aggregates (skandha) constitutes that which is beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This refers to all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas belonging to ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana),
as well as the defiled and indeterminate dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa).
The indeterminate dharmas of all those beyond training,
as well as all unconditioned dharmas,
belong to ordinary beings.
That is to say, excluding those who are learners seeking liberation and those who are afflicted, [the remaining] are—
according to their respective cases—
unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified.
These are the outflows (*āsrava*).
They are designated as eight elements (*dhātu*), eight bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of the mental applications (*manasikāra*) and the aggregates (*skandha*).
Regarding the three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*):
The Abhidharma states:
[It consists of] the defiled views and doubts arising from discrimination, as well as the bases for views and the bases for doubt;

furthermore, it includes the mental concomitants that arise following those views and so forth, the common occurrences and co-occurrences that arise together with those views and so forth, and the verbal and mental karmas produced by those views and so forth.
And all the aggregates, elements, and bases of the evil destinies are the meaning of what is to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
In this context, "view" and "doubt" refer to the bases of view and doubt (*dṛṣṭi-vicikitsā-sthāna*).
This refers to the factors associated with and co-existent with views and doubt, as well as their seeds.
Once the Path of Seeing has been attained, those contaminated factors that are contrary to what is abandoned by seeing are abandoned through cultivation.

That which is contrary to what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) refers to all other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) besides the defiled views and so forth arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
This is because contaminated phenomena include the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), as well as the coarse speech that follows them.
The third fascicle of that treatise states: "Although the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) are accompanied by the heavy residues (dausthulya) of the afflictions,
they are nevertheless established as being of an untainted nature (anāsrava),
because they all pertain to the entire existence."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "other tainted phenomena" (*sāsrava-dharma*), this also includes the wholesome states of the stage of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
That treatise further states:
"That is to say, all tainted phenomena, excluding the wholesome states of penetration."
This is not that which is to be abandoned.
As for the meaning of "the antidote that eternally abandons all defilements," it refers to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Regarding the meaning of "already abandoned":
it refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), wherein the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, have already abandoned their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
therefore, they are called "abandoned."
The following section reveals the meanings of "formless" (*arūpa*) and so forth.
As previously stated, that which is the opposite of the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) and so forth constitutes the "formless" and so forth;
that is to say: formless, invisible, non-obstructive, outflow-free (*anāsrava*), non-contentious (*araṇa*), and so on.
In the Abhidharma treatises, form and formlessness, the visible and the invisible, and the resistant and the non-resistant are explained in terms of their continuity.
This treatise later analyzes formlessness and so forth.
This is because the master of the treatise distinguishes them according to their differing intentions regarding the Dharma.
Below, the fourth section explains the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), their inclusion, and their association;
it consists of five points.
First, the explanation of the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*).
Regarding the phrase "the essence of that which is summoned by various [factors]":
it is like a single material object of form.
It is summoned by various names such as color and fragrance;
this indicates that many dharmas are accumulated in a single location,
just as there is a single mind.

The teaching of various designations such as "feeling" and "perception" is intended to convey that the mind and its mental factors are a collection of many phenomena that function through mutual integration and intermingling.
Just as the four objects, such as visible form and so forth, are mutually blended,
and just as the four aggregates are blended within a single mind,
the general summarized meaning of this category is as follows:
To speak directly, within a single category of body, the five sense organs and their objects are collectively condensed and accumulated.
Furthermore, within a single category of mind, the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors also arise together and accumulate within a single moment of thought.
It is also called a general summary.
Furthermore, as stated in [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] at fifty-three:
"That is to say, whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present, and whether distant or near."
The same applies up to consciousness.
Thus, in brief, the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the sense of a collection or accumulation of all [factors].
As for the meaning of "increase" (*caya*):
Furthermore, based on the differing growth and decline of the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), we explain "accumulation" (*cita*).
Moreover, when wholesome or defiled minds arise, the increase in the number of concomitant mental factors is called "increase";
when neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds arise, the decrease in their number is called "decrease."
Furthermore, since there must be accumulation through augmentation for there to be diminution,
we now cite diminution as proof that accumulation exists.
This is the second explanation of the meaning of "form" (rūpa).

Question: How many are bound exclusively to the desire realm and the form realm? Answer:
Eleven—namely, the five faculties, the three consciousnesses, and the three objects.
This is because fragrance, taste, and two of the consciousnesses belong exclusively to the desire realm.
Seventh, the explanation of the appropriated (*upātta*) and the non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
Jing says: "The five [aggregates] are appropriated."
The five faculties;
the five objects of appropriation and non-appropriation;
and the five sense-objects.
That which is not separated from the sense faculties is grasped by consciousness;
that which is separated from the sense faculties is not appropriated.
The Abhidharma states:
The five [bases], beginning with the eye, consist entirely [of the element] and one part of four [others];

Regarding this, it is said that the five are both "appropriated" (upātta) and "non-appropriated" (anupātta).
Because sound arises without being separated from the sense faculty, it is said to be "appropriated" (upātta).
However, the Abhidharma does not state that it is appropriated because sound is not always present.
As for the remaining [elements] being non-appropriated and so forth:
The remaining seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are entirely non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
As for the other eight elements—namely, those five objects apart from the five sense-faculties and the five sense-faculties themselves—they are [partly] appropriated and [partly] non-appropriated.
Because a separate grasping mind that performs the appropriation (*upādāna*) cannot be found therein;
thus says the Master Ki.
If the ultimate truth of the Mahāyāna is such that only the eighth consciousness is capable of appropriation (*upādāna*),
yet it accords with the gateway of reasoning that it pervades all six consciousnesses.
Now, the force of the subsequent passage states: "Because matter cannot be apprehended apart from those other [elements] that can maintain it.
This follows the logical method;
for the element of sound is not separate from its sense organ and exists constantly.
It is termed "appropriated" (upātta).
Because the sphere of sound is not constant,
it is not discussed here.
Now, regarding its scope:
as for those who claim that the eighth [consciousness] does not take sound and so forth as its objects,
this is as analyzed elsewhere.
Ce says: "That which is apart from those five sense faculties and five external objects—the remaining mental factors—is the appropriator.
It is apprehended as appropriating those faculties and objects."
Therefore, those faculties and objects are what are appropriated.
However, apart from those mind and mental factors,
no other non-mental phenomena serve as the appropriator.
Because it is impossible to find any appropriation (*upādāna*) of those minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
the eight elements (*dhātu*) are non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
Question:

Answer: Because they lack substantial existence (*asvabhāva*).
Unlike the *Prakaraṇapāda*,
this [text] clarifies the distinctions among the elements (*dhātu*) by elucidating the eighteen elements.

Sentient beings are provisional;
the essence of the elements is real.

This refers collectively to the preceding three—the various elements (nānā-dhātu) and the single element—designated as the "immeasurable elements" (apramāṇa-dhātu). Below this...

stating that Chengtai says "akṣa" is the name for the seed-kernel of a fruit.
Its shape resembles a grindstone from this region;
because it exists in immeasurable quantities,
it is not used as a simile.
Since this term does not exist in this region [of China],
the original name is retained. Within the concluding verse, what is the "one"?
Substantial existence has two [categories];
the four alternatives have three;
and the homogeneous character has four.
The five [aggregates] are grasped;
the six [elements] are appropriated; the seven [bases] are not possessed.
The various [elements] and so forth are neither one nor eight.
From here below is the second section, which extensively analyzes the elements through fourteen gates;
first, it analyzes the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*).
Jingyun: These six types herein are all explained according to the "gate of causes and conditions" regarding the seeds of the eighteen realms within the ālayavijñāna.
Below, the establishment of the realms is explained in order to manifest the exclusion of the three conditions.
The establishment of the *dhātu* (elements) is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*), the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*), and so forth.
Alternatively, in terms of the functioning of the eye and other faculties, it has the meaning of "cause" because they exist prior to and give rise to subsequent [moments].
This extends even to the meaning of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*) and so forth.
As it is said that the final eye of an Arhat cannot project a subsequent [moment] and is therefore not a *dhātu*,
one should understand that at other times, the preceding [moment] is able to produce the succeeding one.
Furthermore, it is also called a "realm" (dhātu).
As for the meaning of "cause," it has the sense of "conditioned cause" (hetu-pratyaya).
Regarding the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*):
it is as is said in the world, where that which is capable of directly producing a sprout is called a seed.
Regarding the meaning of "intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti*):
The causal conditions are the intrinsic nature of the fruit.
Regarding the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*):
the fruit is called the lineage because it arises from that source.
Regarding the meaning of "subtle":
the principle of causes and conditions is profound, and is thus termed "subtle.
It exists by virtue of cause and effect.
The term "sustaining" (dhṛti) signifies this meaning.
Alternatively, this may refer to the substance of the eighteen elements as they manifest:
that which can produce what follows is called the "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya).
This explains the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) by way of the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Since the subsequent text explains the eighteen elements (dhātu) to manifest the causal condition,
the twelve bases (āyatana) still exclude three conditions.
Question:
If the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is that which arises later after what has arisen before,
then as with the ten bases (*āyatana*), it would also mean that arising immediately after is the meaning of "base."
The eye of an Arhat after his parinirvāṇa is also not called a "base" (āyatana).
What is the distinction between a "base" and a "constituent" (dhātu)?
The explanation says:
Although their substance is not different, their meanings are always distinct.
For example, regarding the prior eye and the subsequent eye,
there is the aspect of the meaning of "seed."
This is the meaning of "element" (dhātu).
That which causes subsequent growth and development is the meaning of "location" (sthāna).
The statement that, from the perspective of consciousness arising simultaneously with the sense faculty and its object, there are two meanings,
is as follows: for instance, when the eye-faculty and the form-object give rise only to visual consciousness and not to other consciousnesses,
then the eye and the form possess the status of seeds in relation to that visual consciousness.
It is designated as a "seed" in terms of its predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Just as the subsequent arising of the eye was previously explained based on the predominant condition, so too is the seed spoken of therein.
If the simultaneous sense faculty (*indriya*) and object (*viṣaya*) give rise to consciousness, they constitute the meaning of the "base" (*āyatana*).
Therefore, the subsequent treatise asks: "What is the meaning of 'basis' (*āyatana*)?
It is the sense of being the gateway for the arising and growth of all minds and mental factors.
Second, it explains the reason why *nirvāṇa* and *ākāśa* are designated as "elements" (*dhātu*).
Because all sufferings are extinguished through the realization of nirvāṇa,
it is said that one "maintains the non-arising of suffering.
Therefore, nirvāṇa is established within the dharmadhātu.
Space is unimpeded; it sustains the body, enabling its coming and going,
as well as its movements and functions.
Furthermore, space serves as the predominant condition that sustains the eye's function of seeing; therefore,
it is said to sustain the sense of the body's movement and the functions of the eyes and so forth.
Third, the explanation establishing the intent of the *dhātus*:
the eighteen *dhātus* are established to clarify the meaning of causes and conditions;
the term "realm" (*dhātu*) refers precisely to the seeds of the eighteen realms.
Regarding the manifestation of the meaning of the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and their enjoyment:
the faculties are the six faculties,
and the objects are the six objects.
Experience refers to the six consciousnesses and their corresponding agreeable or disagreeable sensations, such as suffering and pleasure.
Briefly stated, there are six kinds of elements (*dhātu*);
extensively, they are immeasurable.
Question: By whom are the eighteen elements (dhātus) distinguished?
Based on what are they distinguished, and how many kinds of elements are there?
Answer: Briefly stated, they are distinguished by way of six kinds, and so forth.
By means of six principles, one distinguishes the various elements (dhātu),
such as the eighteen beginning with the eye;
their essential nature is dharma.
Therefore, it is called the *dharmadhātu*.

The portion of the *dharmadhātu* that consists of the untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*) possessed by those with the dispositions for the three vehicles (*triyānagotra*) is termed the "pure realm" (*viśuddhadhātu*).
Alternatively, it may also be defined in relation to the *dharmadhātu* possessed by those who possess the untainted seed-lineage (*gotra*).
Because they are all supreme and wondrous, they are collectively termed the "Pure Realm" (*viśuddhadhātu*).
Thus, as previously stated, the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) that have existed from the beginningless past are called the "innate realm" (*prakṛtistha-dhātu*);
furthermore, those who abide in the lineages of the three vehicles (*triyānagotra*) and those who do not abide in any lineage are likewise established as being innately possessed [of this nature].
The seed of nirvāṇa is also called the fundamental nature-element (prakṛti-dhātu).
As for the seeds of the defiled and pure realms formed through initial perfuming, which result in superior or inferior births within saṃsāra, these are the seeds of birth produced by new perfuming.
The newly perfumed untainted seeds are called the "nature of the cause of nirvāṇa," and are therefore termed the "perfumed element" (*dhātu*).
When the seeds of the already-arisen element have ceased and entered the past,
they are said to have "already yielded their fruit."
The seeds of fruits that have not yet arisen flow in a constant succession;
they either perish in the past or flow in the present.
Regarding the "name" (*nāman*), which has not yet yielded its fruit,
there are three interpretations of its nature within the *prakṛtadhātu* (nature-element) and *vāsanādhātu* (perfuming-element): those of Vijayabhadra, Ratnakīrti, and Dharmapāla.
One should reflect upon the five pleasures, whether they pertain to the realm of form or the formless realm,
up to and including their non-interruption.
The nineteenth section analyzes the various elements (*dhātu*).
Based on the preceding aggregates (*skandha*), these are established according to their characteristics.
The sixth [section] clarifies the essential nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth.
Jingyun: According to the principles of ultimate truth,
the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses arise from conditions.
If each moment of thought does not persist and lacks any functional activity, how can it see, or even know?

According to the principle of the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), if one speaks of functional activity (*kāritra*), then the sense organs such as the eye are superior in the acts of seeing, hearing, and so forth; thus, it is appropriate to establish "seeing" and so on with respect to them.
Why is this? Because while there are cases where sense-faculties and consciousnesses necessarily arise together,
there are also cases where consciousness exists while the sense-faculties are not fixed.
Since both those with deficient faculties and those with non-deficient faculties can be found, it is said that "the faculties are primary" when establishing [terms] such as "the seer.
In reality, the terms "seer" and so forth are applied only to the act of seeing and so forth;
apart from the acts of seeing, hearing, and so on, there is no separate agent who sees or hears.
Master Ji said:
"As for the statement that 'the intrinsic nature of all phenomena arises from a multitude of conditions, perishes moment by moment,
and lacks causal activity,' this first point is seen as meaning they do not arise spontaneously."
Next, because they are impermanent, one perceives that dharmas lack functional activity;
this is because dharmas with functional activity would contradict the Vaiśeṣika and other such systems.
One cannot see this as a reality.
As for the claim that there may be a flow of consciousness that can be obtained whether the eye and other faculties are deficient or not,
this refers to cases where the seeds of the faculties have been impaired and are thus unable to produce the manifest seeds of consciousness.
The seeds of consciousness are never impaired and flow continuously at all times;
yet, while the sense organs may be deficient or intact,
it is known that if the seeds of the organs exist, they will necessarily give rise to the manifest consciousness.
The arising consciousness possesses its own seeds of consciousness;
however, the seeds of the sense organs do not necessarily produce those organs.
Furthermore, it is said:
The stream [of consciousness] is of a nature similar to consciousness, possessing the three types of accomplishment.
If the faculties are deficient, there is only the maturation of the seeds;
such is the nature of that stream of consciousness.
Since both the presence and absence of intact faculties can be observed,
we know that consciousness arises because of the faculties; it is not the case that the existence of the faculties depends upon the existence of consciousness.
Ce says: "The five consciousnesses have three kinds.
One kind is the maturation of seeds."
Second is the maturation of manifestation;
third is the maturation of mastery.
Therefore, it is said that the flow of the five sense-faculties and their consciousnesses cannot be found.
If the manifest faculties do not exist,
the faculties consist solely of seeds and nothing else.
The basis for these two types is the six sense faculties.
These faculties have a sequential order,
namely, with the eye as the first, and so forth.
The "objects" (viṣaya) are the six sense-fields.
It is said that they have a sequential order, namely:
visible forms, sounds, and so forth.
Both depend upon this consciousness;
consciousness arises depending upon those faculties and objects.
It follows those faculties and those objects.
There is a sequential order:
among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*),
the six consciousnesses arise based on the six sense faculties (*indriyas*) as they take the six objects (*viṣayas*) as their conditions.
Therefore, after explaining the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are taught, followed by the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*).
Thus, it says "three kinds.
As for why this is so, the following section explains the meaning of their mutual dependence.
Among these six types,
first they are explained in prose,
and subsequently summarized in verse.
In the first part, the sequence of the five faculties is established by means of the six causes;
subsequently, the reason why the mental faculty (*manas*) is placed last is explained in general.
Within the first part, the first [section] establishes the order of priority based on the number of objects of perception (*ālambana*).
This means that because what is seen by the eye is most extensive, it is mentioned first;
because what is heard by the ear regarding sounds is more limited, it is mentioned next, and so forth.
These two follow conventional worldly affairs to explain their sequence.
Third, the sequence is distinguished by means of the differences between joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).
Jing says: "This refers to following the joy and bliss of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
First, the eye and the other [faculties] are explained.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Ya" refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Master Ji said:

Next, regarding vocal karma:
when receiving solid food, one first smells its fragrance and then tastes its flavor.
The subsequent [senses], such as touch and so forth,

The first five objects are exclusively present;
