The tenth point clarifies that one can give rise to the vitarka and vicāra of a lower stage while in a higher stage.

Regarding the response that this occurs because the seeds of all consciousnesses accompanied by vitarka and vicāra follow along with the concentration free from vitarka and vicāra, such that they manifest once one has emerged from that concentration:
Jingyun: The five consciousnesses do not, in fact, correspond with vitarka and vicāra;

It is not that those three consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra.

Therefore, when one in a higher stage wishes to give rise to the three types of sensory consciousness belonging to a lower stage, one must necessarily give rise to the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) of the lower stage to simultaneously apprehend visible forms and other objects.
Therefore, the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra states:
"When a single atom gives rise to a single consciousness,
at that time, the conceptualizing manovijñāna arises together with those five consciousnesses, taking the same object as their cognitive domain."
Therefore, it is known that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) which arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses must necessarily be associated with vitarka and vicāra,
because it is designated as "discriminative.
Furthermore, it was previously established that vitarka and vicāra are associated exclusively with the feelings of displeasure (daurmanasya) and joy (saumanasya).
It does not state that [the five consciousnesses] are associated with suffering or pleasure;
from this, it can be known that the five consciousnesses definitely lack vitarka and vicāra. Ji says:
In this context, it is the mind accompanied by vitarka and vicāra that acts as the inducer, drawing forth the arising of the five sensory consciousnesses;
it is not as the Śrāvaka schools maintain, where the five sensory consciousnesses themselves possess vitarka and vicāra in order to arise.
Because, by means of the path of antidote,
or having become weary and detached,
one eliminates discursive thought and investigation as well as desire.
It is called "detachment from intrinsic nature" and "absence of vitarka and vicāra.
There are types [of dharmas] that exist by virtue of their activity.
Nor is there any fault here.
One should raise this objection:
vitarka and vicāra are bound to the first dhyāna.
The second dhyāna arises through detachment from desire;
the second dhyāna is said to be detached from the faculty of suffering.
Within the second dhyāna, suffering arises.
The faculty of suffering is the fruit of unwholesome karma and is oppressive;
in the second dhyāna there is no faculty of suffering;
and vitarka and vicāra give rise to the three consciousnesses.
For this reason, in the higher stages there are vitarka and vicāra;
the eleven [faculties]— the eye, ear, and nose— each produce two parts,
while the remaining ones produce only one.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are two meanings:
first, for the physical beauty and dignity of the body;
second, for the clarity of consciousness.
In this context, one point is abbreviated:
although the visual, auditory, and olfactory consciousnesses arise based on two [bases], the substance of the consciousness itself is singular.
This means that if one eye is afflicted, the visual consciousness becomes unclear.
Thus, one knows that a single consciousness relies upon two eyes.
Furthermore, since consciousness is not material form, it lacks spatial location; therefore, the drawing forth [of objects] cannot be established as having three parts.
This distinguishes [the view] from that of the Vātsīputrīyas, the Sthaviras, and others, who maintain that two eyes can successively produce a single consciousness.
Thirteen [sections] clarify the meaning of cause and effect. Jing says:
This question is identical to the objection raised by the Sautrāntika masters:
that just as the two horns of an ox exist simultaneously and are not related as cause and effect in relation to one another, so it is here.
The same applies to the eye faculty and the visual consciousness being coexistent.
The intended meaning of the answer here is that consciousness arises in dependence upon the eye.
It is not like the arising of a sprout upon the cessation of a seed. Why is this?
Because the eye and visual consciousness are not the direct causes of its arising.
Therefore, cause and effect exist simultaneously, just like the light and the lamp.
Question:
The seeds of the Mahāyāna possess six characteristics simultaneously.
All phenomena that arise do so simultaneously.
Why, then, do you not cite this principle,
but instead answer by saying that consciousness arises depending on the eye, unlike the case where a sprout arises when a seed has perished?
The answer says:
Maitreya, for the time being, follow the tenets of the Sautrāntika school:
the cause precedes and the effect follows.
Just as the cessation of the seed and the emergence of the sprout illustrate the principle of cause and effect,
it is therefore said that the eye and visual consciousness are not the direct causes of one another's arising, but exist merely as established bases;
this is what is meant by such a statement.
Vasumitra cites this passage to state that the eye and visual consciousness are simultaneous, yet the former is not the direct cause of the latter's arising;
he thus establishes that a present entity possesses two temporal functions,
just as a present seed produces its "arising-characteristic" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) at a different moment from its own distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
When manifest dharmas arise in the present, this very arising is termed "abiding";
therefore, the duration of abiding is not distinct from the moment of arising.
As a dharma is about to perish and undergoes decay, it is termed "alteration."

Therefore, all instances where cause and effect arise through mutual production take the moment of distinct characteristics in the present as the cause and the moment of the characteristic of arising as the fruit.
As for what the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* calls "simultaneous existence" (*sahabhū*):
Because cause and effect coexist in the present, they are said to be "simultaneously existing" (sahabhū), which is not the same as the characteristic of simultaneous arising (sahajātalakṣaṇa).
This principle is not employed in the West;
therefore, they refute it, saying:
When you establish the characteristic of difference, is the dharma at the time of its existence one with or different from the dharma at the time of its arising?
If they are one, there would be no time of difference;
if they are different, there must be a distinct substantial entity.
Master Ji said:
"In this context, what is called the 'establishing cause' (pratisthā-hetu) is the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)."
It is not a direct cause (*samanantarapratyaya*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), what prevents its cause and effect from arising simultaneously?
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Even though one's own seeds exist, because this support is absent, consciousness should not arise."
Its primary cause of arising is indeterminate,
because a seed produces a seed at a different time;
as stated in the previous *Maulī Bhūmi*, section five, regarding the production of a similar [seed] from a different moment.
It is not that this very moment produces a different kind of manifestation;
furthermore, they arise simultaneously.
Fourteen: Clarifying the meaning of the existence, non-existence, and determinacy or indeterminacy of the various elements, such as the eye-element and others, within the three realms.
First, regarding the desire realm:
although sound has interruptions, [it is nonetheless continuous].
However, with respect to a single lifetime, there is definitely the sense of arising.
Next, regarding the higher realms,
it is as the text states.
The concluding verses for the lower categories are likewise present. Jing says:
"Regarding the statement 'skillfulness in the matters of the realms' up to the *Udāna* verse..."
Based on this concluding text,
the preceding analysis of skill in the aggregates is completed;
it should be understood that there is one verse in total that summarizes [the section].
In this text, why is there no concluding summary?
It is simply because the fifth section of the five-part verse— the passage refuting attachments—
states that "the five lineages are not established," and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "The skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*) should be understood as being likewise," this is an analogical explanation of the Mahāyāna.
For the sake of textual convenience, it is presented here in advance; the concluding summary will follow after the section on skill in the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*).
Master Ji said:
"The skillful [verses] at the end summarize the preceding text."
The same applies to the elements (*dhātu*). Bei says:
"Skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana*)."
At the outset, a verse should have been composed, but it was omitted for brevity.
Now, following the previous text, the first *udāna* regarding skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) states:
"The intrinsic nature, the meaning, and the distinctions."
The sequential summary of the bases follows;
the subsequent prose commentary on these six gates and so forth is like the skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*).
It should be understood that at the beginning of the skill in the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*), a summary verse (*uddāna*) should likewise be recited.
This has been omitted for brevity.
How so? Below, in the third section, is the discernment of skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana*).
Among these, there are six [points].
First is the substance of the source. Jing says:
Once the fifth stage within the womb has passed,
one is said to have "attained the eye";
this state remains unimpaired until birth in the formless realm occurs.
This is called "not abandoning.
With the exception of the eye of an Arhat,
all that precedes this, within the substance of the uninterrupted [stream], is not a phenomenon subject to annihilation.
This is the essence of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*). Question:
Why must it be that which arises immediately prior [to the consciousness] in order to be considered a "base"?
The eye that has been extinguished and the eye of an Arhat after parinirvāṇa—these dharmas of extinction are not termed "bases" (*āyatana*).
The commentary explains:
as stated in the following text, the meaning of being a "gate for growth and arising" is the meaning of a "base."
Only when the preceding [moment] can produce the subsequent one in immediate succession does it accord with the meaning of "arising and growing. For this reason:
The eye of an Arhat after [attaining parinirvāṇa] is not called a "base" (āyatana).
The remaining eleven bases should be understood accordingly. Cè says:
The eye has three meanings:
first, the eye;
second, the sense-base of the eye.
Regarding the three bases of eye-contact:
all eyes that are currently manifest are collectively termed "eye";
only those capable of producing subsequent eyes are designated as the "eye-base."

Therefore, when an Arhat’s final eye and other faculties of the desire or form realms cease at death and he is reborn in the formless realm, those final eyes and so forth are not designated as "bases" (āyatana).
The treatise states: "In its essential nature, the uninterrupted [continuum] is not a phenomenon subject to annihilation."
The intention lies herein.
Second, a general explanation of the distinctions between the bases (*āyatana*) and the base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Regarding the answer that "the bases are as previously explained":
That which has already been attained is not abandoned; its essence is not a phenomenon of annihilation.
What is called the "sphere of contact" (spraṣṭavyāyatana) refers to that which is concomitant with contact, arising simultaneously as the faculty that produces that contact.
Regarding the statement that "it can immediately induce various contacts (*sparśa*)":
although the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) of the preceding moment do not coexist with contact, they are able to immediately induce contact in the subsequent moment;
because they are conducive to the subsequent contact, they are also designated as the "sphere of contact" (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Third, the eye that is drawn forth is analyzed in relation to the four propositions. Jing says:
"The subsequent eye of an Arhat."
This is a dharma of annihilation.
When a trainee is born in the formless realm,
this too is a dharma of uninterrupted annihilation.
Furthermore, one who studies [the path] will attain nirvana in this very body.
While the body remains in the desire realm, the eye-faculty is struck and destroyed by another;
at that time, it is the final moment of the eye.
It is also a phenomenon that is uninterrupted and non-ceasing;
it is an improper locus for the eye,
as the ear, nose, and so forth are drawn along immediately thereafter.
In this case, it is not the eye itself that exists;
rather, it is the continuity of the eye.
Furthermore, when an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) dies in the two lower realms and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [the eye does not exist].

as well as those in training (*śaikṣa*) residing in the desire realm whose lives are not yet exhausted and whose eyes have likewise been destroyed.
The final eyes relinquished by such individuals are not termed phenomena that undergo uninterrupted cessation.
Because there are eyes that can produce those [subsequent moments] at a later time, they are all included in the category of "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*).
By this principle, it should be understood that the two systems of the *dhātus* and *āyatanas* do not exhaustively encompass all phenomena;
for instance, the final moments of the eye and so forth are not included within the *dhātus*.
Master Ji said:
"Therefore, within the realm [of form], the eye that is not of the realm refers only to the final momentary eye of an Arhat.
Now, in this context, the eye that is both of the realm and not of the realm also includes the eye of one born in the Formless Realm at the very last moment."
Because one grasps the seeds of the elements within the elements, only the Arhat is mentioned;
however, in this context, since it refers to their manifestation in the present, it is stated generally that the eye-faculty ceases in the subsequent moment.

The fourth [section] consists of a formulation of propositions regarding the mutual relationship between the sphere of discernment (*prativijñapti*) and the sphere of contact (*sparśa*). This is the "consecutive" (*anuloma*) formulation.
Question: What is the difference between this and the distinction previously made in the second [section] regarding the spheres of discernment and contact?

here, the formulation of propositions is used to analyze it specifically.
However, it is not the case that there are no dharmas that are subject to immediate cessation;
this excludes the final eye-faculties and so forth of an Arhat,

Regarding the statement that "if one is in the form realm (rūpadhātu) up to the point of being definitely in an improper place," the Tripiṭaka Master says:

That which is called "inappropriate" (asthāna) refers to those born in the form realm who possess both the nose and tongue faculties,
as well as those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva).
The five faculties, such as the eye, are necessarily incapable of producing the mind and mental factors throughout the course of a single lifetime;
therefore, they are not called *āyatanas*.
Consequently, the subsequent text states that the sense-bases (*āyatana*) are defined by the meaning of being the "gateways for the growth and arising" of all minds and mental factors.
Ce said: This text is erroneous and incomplete;

Fifth, the explanation of the meaning of *āyatana*.
First, the locus is distinguished through question and answer;
subsequently, it is analyzed in detail and its sequence is shown to be identical to that of the *dhātu*.
In the preceding section,
two questions were asked:
first, a question regarding the meaning of the locus.
Second, the establishment of the basis for the question.
The answer consists of two parts:
first, the response to the preceding question.
The six meanings are termed "bases" (*sthāna*).
Briefly summarized, there are three categories.
The meaning of "simultaneous basis" refers to the place of residence.
Second is the prior time,
which is the stage of the preparatory means for the gateway of growth;
third encompasses both times.
It is that which serves as the basis for the nature of integration (*saṃghātatva*).
Regarding the meaning of "gate of production and growth" (*janmanirvṛttidvāra*), the old translation stating it means "gate of flow" (*srotas*) is incorrect; rather, it means "place" (*sthāna*).

If one explains the meaning as "Gate of Departure" (*niḥsaraṇa*), [the same logic applies].
In the Sanskrit original, it should be named *prātihārya*.
The second answer addresses the subsequent question:
the meaning of "place" (*sthāna*) is established for the sake of three purposes.
That is to say, among the twelve bases (āyatana), the mind-base (manāyatana) is the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya);
the five sense organs are the dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya);
and the six objects are the objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya).
Sixth, the analysis of the summary of names and categories (*nāma-sthāna-saṃgraha*).
Within this, first there is the analysis of the summary of alternative names,
followed by the indication of the elements (*dhātu*) through other gates.

The eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth mentioned previously are subsumed within the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) among the twelve sense-spheres.
At that time, the mind-king is the sense-base of mind (manāyatana);
the factors arising simultaneously with the mind-base are the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
With the exception of the state of non-perception (asaṃjñika), these are subsumed within those ten sense-bases, excluding smell and taste.
The subsequent passage states, "Furthermore, as for the basis of the location, it is like the [respective] realms.
This means that within the preceding section on the classification of realms (*dhātu-mukha*), having concluded the explanation of the inclusion of various synonymous names for the realms,
the question and answer now distinguish the nose-realm (*ghrāṇa-dhātu*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) as the basis that makes the physical body majestic and beautiful.
Furthermore, because one has not yet abandoned desire for these two,
and in order to demonstrate that each of the three faculties gives rise to two [types of results] so as to make them majestic based upon this,
this meaning should now be explained in this intermediate section.
This is explained according to the *Dhātunirdeśa*.
Below this is the fourth section, the exposition on skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).
Within this, there is first a brief analysis by way of nine gates.
The subsequent section refers back to what has already been explained in the "Local Basis" (*mūla-bhūmi*) and will not be presented again here.
Within that prior section, first,
the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) were analyzed as being solely phenomena (*dharma*) and devoid of a person (*pudgala*).
The "Cloud of Radiance" (Jingyun) states that there is no sovereign and no agent or experiencer.
This is received [as an exposition] to refute the Sāṃkhya masters' attachment to a self as the experiencer.
This also refutes the Vaiśeṣika masters' attachment to a self as both the agent and the experiencer.
It now clarifies that only causes can act and only effects can experience;
there is no self-exerting agency.
The Vaiśeṣika masters establish the category of "existence" (*sat*), asserting that when all phenomena arise, there exists a real functional activity (*kāritra*).
Now it is clarified that all phenomena lack such real activity;
they do not attain independence but arise from causes and proceed in dependence upon a multitude of conditions.
This refutes the non-Buddhist view of spontaneity (*svabhāva*),
which holds that all phenomena exist spontaneously and are not produced from causes. Here,
it is clarified that [phenomena] arise from causes and conditions and do not possess independence.
To know that things are not spontaneous,
that they exist where there was originally nothing, and that having existed they disperse and perish—
this refutes the calculation of permanence.
Now, it is clarified that because of this,
impermanence is manifested solely by phenomena (*dharma*).
This concludes the initial section on the absence of a sovereign (*anīśvara*) and so forth.
"Only dharmas can moisten that which is to be moistened.
This concludes the preceding section. Second, [dharmas] lack any activity of their own.
It is solely through ignorance that there are formations and existence;
they lack any real functional activity,
yet they fall within the continuum.
This concludes the third transformation;
[now for] the fourth. Ji says:
To say that there is no functional activity means,
for instance, that Īśvara [is inactive],
or that this phenomenon arises from conditions and lacks its own inherent activity.
The rest is understandable.
Regarding the two explanations within this:
First, the difference in terminology is explained:
because the substance of the cause acts as a condition capable of producing an effect,
the cause is termed "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
Because the substance of the fruit arises through the power of those conditions,
it is said that "fruit" is named "dependently arisen.
Next, we shall distinguish the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*) by way of their mutual production.
Regarding the phrase "because this latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) exists without being abandoned," this explains the cause by the name "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
Regarding the phrase "that entanglement of ignorance (avidyā-paryavasthāna) exists":
This is called "fruit" and "dependently arisen.
Regarding the statement, "Because this is produced by the entanglement of ignorance,

those formations proceed," this explains that the cause is named "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) and the fruit is named "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna), based on the conditionality of formations upon ignorance.
If, in this way, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) arise because their seeds are not severed,
this explains dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*) by means of formations arising from the seeds of formations.
Because the various formations arise, there is the evolution of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because the seeds [of consciousness] arise from the perfuming of consciousness by formations (*saṃskāra*),
they draw forth those seeds of consciousness and cause them to increase.
This passage explains dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*) in terms of formations as the condition for consciousness.
Regarding "the remaining [categories] are likewise," one should understand them by analogy with what has been stated above.
Third, the distinction between the provisional and the real.
Jingyun said:
"That which has birth and death is provisional,
because it is by means of the dharma of non-arising."
The preceding members of the causal chain, moistened by craving and grasping, are established as "existence" (bhava).
Birth, aging, and death are merely conventional designations applied to the states of phenomena within the subsequent retribution;
therefore, they are established as being nominal.
Tai Chè states that "birth" and "old age and death" are the names of three of the four characteristics;
because they are provisional designations based on temporal stages.
Nor is it real. The Four Clarities establish dependent origination through five aspects.
First, they are raised collectively, then interrogated, and finally enumerated.
The subsequent section provides a detailed, sequential explanation.
Within the preceding [section],
the first point is that observing the arising of the six sense bases constitutes the prior removal of the fruit of suffering.
From delusion regarding this suffering, the seven [factors] beginning with ignorance arise.
Second, there is the manifest branch of feeling (*vedanā*).
Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and the three types of existence (*bhava*) arise from attachment to this feeling, it serves as the cause for birth.
These are the causal bases for birth.
"Three" refers to the preceding seven links;
"four" refers to craving, clinging, and existence.
The fifth refers to two [factors] of the future.
Thus, these twelve aspects arise through mutual causality in an uninterrupted succession.
Within this, the twelve links are explained as three divisions.
First, the first seven members constitute the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Second, the second and third members constitute the productive cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*).
Third, the two future members are the fruits of these two aforementioned causes—the projecting and the productive.
In the Abhidharma, there are four categories.
As in the previous case of the seven [factors], these are divided into the "projecting" and the "projected";
in the latter five, they are divided into the "producing" and the "produced."
In the separate explanation, it says:
"That which arises as the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) with name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as its condition within the present life refers to the substance of the locus."
"Not knowing the non-interruption [of the continuum] is what is called ignorance.
Because one is deluded regarding the six sense bases, ignorance arises;
with ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise, continuing on until the stage of contact.
This explains the meaning of the "basis" (āśraya).
From here on, the basis is concluded. Ji, Ce, and others say:
This collectively identifies the name-and-form and the six sense-bases of a single body as the basis for the drawing-forth causes of ignorance and so forth;
it does not refer to temporal divisions.
Ignorance, contact, and feeling constitute the basis for the arising causes of manifold sufferings.
In terms of temporal sequence,
contact and feeling serve as the basis and cause for the arising of craving, grasping, and so forth;
they are the basis and cause for the arising of all suffering.
This also establishes the essential nature and explains the meaning of the connection:

"The causes that lead to all sufferings, up to the suffering of old age and death," because they are perfumed by those factors of the dependent origination consisting of the three types of karmic formations, such as merit and so forth.
The five factors that project [rebirth] increase as seeds,
capable of projecting the future fruits of the remaining five factors— consciousness and so forth, including birth and old age and death.
Therefore, it concludes below.
The cause for the arising of all suffering refers to "feeling conditions craving, craving conditions grasping, grasping conditions becoming," and so forth.

Regarding the nature of the cause of production, it is explained below as "that which was previously performed. There is an interpretation [which states]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
This means that the previously formed factors of the formations (*saṃskāra*) and the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth are moistened by the afflictions (*kleśa*);
as the fruit is about to manifest through their conjunction,
it is therefore called "one's own" (*svaka*).
The arising of manifold suffering refers to the fact that with birth as condition there is aging-and-death.
This extracts the essence of manifold suffering;
that is to say, from consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth, until it again receives the designation of "suffering."
The five-membered seeds previously existed within consciousness and were termed "projecting causes" (*ākṣepa-hetu*);
at the present time, when they produce their fruit, they are termed "birth and old age and death.
Furthermore, these seeds are the maturation (*vipāka*) that constitutes the very substance of birth and death.
It is also given the name "suffering.
Fifth, the analysis of ignorance:
herein, the correct meaning is first set forth.
Next, the refutation of false attachments;
finally, the conclusion of the correct meaning. Within this refutation of attachments, there is further refutation of attachments.
First, there is a general refutation of the two attachments;
subsequently, there is a specific refutation of the two attachments.
Regarding the former:
It is not that the absence of wisdom is itself ignorance, nor is it that one who possesses wrong knowledge is ignorance; rather, there is a teaching that the very absence of wisdom is ignorance,
which exists as a distinct entity of its own.
The subsequent explanation states that deviant wisdom (mithyājñāna) which contradicts the correct [path] is itself ignorance (avidyā).
Where else, then, could there be a separate essence of ignorance?
Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific refutations,
the question "Why is this so? represents the intention of the opponent's inquiry.
It is precisely the principle that my establishment of "clarity" (*vidyā*) and "erroneous cognition" (*mithyājñāna*) as the essence of ignorance (*avidyā*) is correct.
Why do you not agree with me?
Below, the Master of the Treatise refutes this.
First, the existence [of intrinsic nature] is refuted to clarify its non-existence; subsequently, erroneous cognition is refuted.
Within the former, six kinds of faults are revealed.
First, there is the fault that the three categories would not be established. Jing said:
"If that clarity were itself non-ignorance (avidyā), then [the categories would fail]."
The clarification that ignorance is itself the absence of intrinsic nature means that dharmas devoid of intrinsic nature possess no three grades;
yet the Buddha has categorized ignorance as superior, middling, and inferior.
Therefore, one should know that ignorance is not [simply] non-ignorance.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"The ignorance you posit must lack an essential nature (*svabhāva*)."
Because the three grades do not exist,
it is like a rabbit's horn.
Beiyun said:
Because this measure does not accord with the meaning of the text, it is now established anew:
according to your position, ignorance (avidyā) should have no three grades,
because it is of the nature of ignorance.
Like the horns of a rabbit and so forth.
Second, the fallacy that there would be no distinction between manifest [consciousness] and seeds: that is to say, if manifestation did not exist.
If non-existence were clearly established as being without intrinsic nature,
how could there be the distinction between the two types— the seed and the manifest?
This is because phenomena that lack intrinsic nature have identical characteristics at all times.
Because there would be no manifest activity nor seeds remaining as latent bonds.
Third, all minds would be defiled, which would result in the loss [of the distinction between them];
that is to say, if it were answered that ignorance is simply the absence of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
In the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the minds of the three natures all reach a state where they lack the clarity of wisdom.
Consequently, the mental factors (*caitta*) of these three natures should all become defiled,
because that ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself a defiled phenomenon.
The fault of not being subsumed within the four meanings:
that is to say, if there were no "emptiness," then there would be no "nature.
A dharma devoid of nature is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it cannot be defiled, nor can it be purified.
Fifth, the non-arising of the light of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*).
This means that for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the mental factors of the three natures are all ignorance (*avidyā*).
As long as ignorance continues in succession, the light of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā-āloka*) can certainly not arise.
The sixth is the fault of the noble ones’ false speech:
namely, that one should not say that because ignorance ceases, knowledge arises;
for dharmas that are unarisen do not undergo arising or cessation.
The following section refutes erroneous views through wisdom.
First, three gateways are raised as challenges;
subsequently, each is refuted in successive order.
Previously, I also refuted that position by means of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
If, apart from untainted clarity (*anāsrava-vidyā*), all the wisdom of the three natures possessed by ordinary worldlings were also false wisdom (*mithyājñāna*),
then there would be no distinction between the natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
Because all [of these] are based on false cognition, they are not reasonable.
Next, I shall refute their tenets by means of the nature of false adherence and cognition.
There are three difficulties. First is the difficulty that [wrong knowledge] would be indistinguishable from [wrong] view (*dṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, if only defiled cognition characterized by false adherence were called wrong knowledge, then...
This is because only the five views are designated as being of a defiled nature.
According to the principles of the Buddha’s Dharma,
the five false views arise through the power of ignorance.
The conceptualization of names as distinct entities is called "clinging.
It would be illogical for the five views themselves to be ignorance;
however, those five views are not separate from ignorance.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*) differ in their modes of activity;
therefore, it is illogical to designate defiled cognition as ignorance.
Second, the objection regarding contradiction with the scriptures.
That is to say, if ignorance were not distinct from its characteristics,
the Blessed One would not have established the latent tendency of views as something separate from ignorance among the seven latent tendencies.
Regarding the seven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*:

first, the latent disposition of sensual desire; second, aversion; third, attachment; fourth, pride; fifth, ignorance; sixth, views; and seventh, doubt. It is difficult to find any scriptural source that enumerates them as three.
The understanding [of this] may be known from the text itself.
Below, there are four faults involved in refuting [the opponent's position] by means of false knowledge associated with afflictions (*kleśa*).
The first is the fault that it does not coexist with [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Second, there is the fault that [the wisdom] would not be the leader;
third, there is the fault that the defilement of nature would not be established.
That is to say, it could also be argued that the wisdom defiled by nature is so because of its association with the defilement of association.
It cannot be said that what is not the essence of ignorance constitutes the nature of ignorance.
Nor is it a fault that the four inversions are not afflictions;
for example, just as the feeling, perception, volition, and so forth associated with other afflictions do not themselves constitute the nature of those afflictions.
It cannot be said that ignorance becomes an affliction through association;
nor can it be said that what is not of the nature of ignorance now becomes "knowledge."
Sixth, explaining its practice.
Jing says: "In this section, the function of the factor of practice (*pratipad-aṅga*) is analyzed."
This clarifies two kinds of threefold formations (*triprakāra-saṃskāra*).
First, regarding the clarification that bodily formation (*kāya-saṃskāra*) is twofold:
the winds of inhalation and exhalation are called bodily formation.
The vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) has two meanings.
First, it serves as the activity for the retribution body (*vipākakāya*).
Second, from the third dhyāna downward, because of the presence of the vital wind, the body remains sustained and does not perish.
Second, they serve as the movement for bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Because bodily action is set in motion by the power of wind,
one knows that bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*) are so called because if the substance of that bodily action is itself a factor of formation (*saṃskāra*), it is therefore termed "bodily formation."
Second, the actions performed by the body are also called bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*).
When a deluded person commits acts such as killing,
they first give rise to the bodily winds that accompany the action.
Only after that does one initiate defiled bodily action.
Next, speech and mind are explained:
vitarka and vicāra are the volition that initiates speech.
It is called "vocal formation" (*vāg-abhisamskāra*).
The substance of the vocal karma produced [by it] is itself a member of the formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) and is also called "formation.
Combining these two types, they are collectively termed "vocal formation."
Perception, volitional formations, feeling,
and intention are all causes of the sovereign mind;
they are termed mental formations (*manasaṃskāra*).
Mental volition (cetanā) is precisely the essential nature of the constituent of formations (saṃskāra);
therefore, it is called "formations. Ji says:
Among these, the wind of cessation is called bodily formation (*kāya-saṃskāra*).
It is by means of this wind that the various bodily forms continue in succession.
For example, one who dies in a narrow space is said to be dead because the winds of inhalation and exhalation no longer circulate.
Furthermore, there is the wind that acts as the primary cause for the transformation of bodily karma and so forth; herein lie two meanings.
Another interpretation holds that this refers to a single condition alone.
The explanation states:
The winds of inhalation and exhalation are called "the practitioner.
This is a general statement identifying wind as the primary guide;
the following provides the explanation for why this is so.
This is because it must be through the bodily action (*kāyakarman*) associated with wind that [the movement] proceeds.
Seventh, the explanation of the realms and stages (*dhātubhūmi*). Jing says:
Just as the present body experienced by one born in the desire realm constitutes birth, aging, and death,
so too— referring to this very body that undergoes birth and death— the first ten links are all subsumed within the desire realm.
Up to and including birth, one is born into the perception of compassion;
because old age and death are subsumed under their fruit,
their causes are likewise included within the perception of compassion.

Since this is so, ignorance belonging to a lower realm does not give rise to karma of a higher realm; when an ordinary person who has not yet abandoned desire gives rise to the karma of the *anāgamya* concentration, it is produced solely by the seeds of ignorance belonging to that very level.
Now, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
the ignorance of a lower stage can give rise to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of a higher stage; therefore,
it is known that his interpretation contradicts the treatise.
Bei says: This limb of existence is judged in relation to the place of rebirth;
thus, it may be bound to that place of rebirth.
This consists of only one limb of existence.
It does not arise from the twelve links of dependent origination.

The eight [links] subsume the twelve links by way of three matters. Furthermore, as for the passage "up to all being subsumed under matter": *Note: This translation assumes the context of a commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* or a similar Abhidharma treatise concerning the categorization of the twelve links of dependent origination.*
Among these, two members of the [twelvefold] dependent origination are mental karma.
Within the member of formations (*saṃskāra*), both seeds and active manifestations are the member of formations.
As for the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it takes as its essence the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) that are inherently present within consciousness itself.
Regarding the statement that the seeds of the factors of conditioned origination (saṃskāra) are called the factor of consciousness (vijñāna):
because the seeds of the saṃskāras reside within consciousness, they share its basis and are therefore also termed "consciousness."
Regarding the intrinsic nature of the consciousness link, its inclusion within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is indeterminate, being subject to the preferences of various commentators.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "among the two types of karma, up to what is called existence" (*bhava*):
the former refers to karma among the projecting causes (*ākṣepahetu*).
The latter refers to karma among the causes of arising.
Regarding "craving and grasping" among the three afflictions, Jing and Bei both state: [text missing].
Upon first reading this text,
it appears that as craving and grasping arise in the present, they trigger karma; consequently,
there must be the "falling away" of the past, which is designated as ignorance and formations.
This reasoning is not correct.

now, because it is moistened by craving and grasping, it is further designated as "existence" (bhava).
This explains that "moistening" (ārdraṇa) is synonymous with "arousing" (samudācāra).
Master Ji further states:
"The term 'arising' (utpāda) means 'birth' (jāti)."
Because they are able to produce existence (*bhava*),
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are also called "initiators";
they are not the afflictions that initiate karma.

this refers to the fact that, in terms of the seeds of the names and words of the five branches, these are exclusively the cause for future suffering.
Furthermore, it refers to the contact and sensation within those very five branches.

If the five present members are taken as the five manifest fruits, then these are the results of old age and death produced by the ten past members acting as causes; within this present cycle of birth and death, they are differentiated into consciousness.
Furthermore, regarding the five members subsumed under the present fruit, up to the dependent origination subsumed under the cause,
Jing says: "The reason the five members of the present are called 'fruit' is as follows."
That is to say, the past ten causes that produce the fruits of birth and old age and death are divided into five branches.
As for the two future branches designated as "fruits," these are the names of the fruits of the present ten causes.

Ce says: "The preceding consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling were previously termed 'the nature of seeds' and 'the names for the drawing-in causes of manifold sufferings.
Therefore, we know that these five present factors are not being described in terms of seeds."
Now, it is said that the five members subsumed under the present fruit and the two members of the future are collectively termed "subsumed under the fruit.
Thus, one should know that the five members of the present are also collectively subsumed under the presently arising fruition of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
The two branches are said to be five branches;
that is, they include both active manifestations and seeds.
The same applies to the others as well.
The masters of the West say:
the five members of the present [time] primarily establish the seeds while also including the active manifestations;
the two members of the future [time] primarily establish the active manifestations while also mentioning the seeds.
The ninth [section] distinguishes the inability to clarify the arising of the five dharmas and the formation of the five faults.
Within this, the first part clarifies the arising of the five dharmas,
and the latter part clarifies the five kinds of faults.
In the preceding section, the number was raised, the names were listed, and they were explained in sequence.
First, ignorance regarding the three time periods gave rise to doubt;
thus it is said: "If one is perplexed as to whether this belongs to someone internally..."
This killing of the internal body in the present moment—even though it is my own possession—who am I? As for who I am: [I am not this].
This doubt concerns to whom the present internal body belongs;
as for the question of where this sentient being will go and abide in the future,
it concerns the place from which the present sentient being comes and to which they go.
It should be understood that this doubt arises from ignorance regarding the two limits—the past and the future—within the present.
Second, from the three types of delusion concerning the internal, external, and so forth, four kinds of craving arise.
First, one generates craving for the internal body within the present.
Next, regarding the future, there arises craving for renewed existence within one's own body.
Next, regarding external objects already obtained in the present, there arises craving accompanied by joy and lust.
Regarding external objects not yet obtained in the future, there arises craving for various joys and pleasures.
The three types of karma and their maturation are both objects of delusion that can give rise to dwelling in improper places.
Rudra is translated here as "Violent and Evil."
Viṣṇu— formerly called Bīnìtiān (Vishnu Tian)—
is translated here according to his delusive functions;
he is able, through his delusive power, to manifest as elephants, horses, and so forth for the sake of the deluded world.
This deity is entirely a transformation-body of Maheśvara;
some say it is Viṣṇu,
which is a transformation-body of the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha.
The Lord of the World (Lokapāla) is none other than Mahābrahmā.
All these sentient beings, deluded regarding the fruits of their own karma, are born from that heaven.
Therefore, one takes refuge in and develops reverent faith toward those heavens;
fourth, there is the ignorance regarding the improper comprehension of the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths, as well as the various views arising from that ignorance;
fifth, there is the ignorance regarding cause and effect and the spheres of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), which can give rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*).
Among these, the first clarifies how delusion regarding cause and effect gives rise to worldly overweening pride (*adhimāna*);
this refers to the overweening pride of one who, regarding that which is not the abiding state of the heavens, claims it to be the true cause.
Next, it clarifies how delusion regarding the spheres of contact (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) gives rise to worldly overweening pride.

This means that when one attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya through the Path, it is essential to realize the emptiness of the six bases of contact and to bring name-and-form (nāmarūpa) to its ultimate end before one can attain finality.
Now, those non-Buddhists do not realize this; their claim to have realized it is an overweening pride (abhimāna).
The five dharmas have been explained above;
now there are nineteen types of delusion (*moha*),
which, when combined with what was previously stated, constitute seven categories.
Now, summarizing those that arise within the five dharmas, they constitute the five delusions.
From here on, the five faults are clarified;
first, the five kinds of defilements produced are restated and concluded.
The following clarifies the five faults that arise from these five [types of] attainment.
First, one harbors self-doubt and indecision, following the false teachings of others to throw oneself from cliffs or leap into fire, thereby undergoing much suffering in the present life;
this is clearly explained in the middle three sections.

Fifth, because one gives rise to the overweening pride (*abhimāna*) of having practiced the correct means when practicing non-means such as self-starvation, one fails to attain rebirth in the heavens;
even falling into the evil destinies is termed a "discordant fruit" (*visadṛśaphala*).
Because there is, in reality, no penetration,
one who has not attained the wisdom regarding the six sense bases yet claims to have attained it gives rise to overweening pride;
therefore, there is no untainted fruit of the śramaṇa.
The End of the Fifteenth Scroll, Part Two, of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*.
